name: Hod
blurb: One storage system that keeps every Sims 1 file byte-perfect forever, and the tools that read and write it: a browser you can open anything in, a save editor that can't lose your game, and eventually a community exchange. A hod carries bricks so you can build; hodós is Greek for path. Both fit.

stats.label: file formats read and rewritten byte-for-byte
references mapped across the whole store
lots, every one with its own house picture

pillars.body: Open anything. Every file inspectable down to the byte — structure, references, where it came from.
Edit safely. Every change is a new version; undo is the storage model, not a prayer.
Lists like playlists, packs built in the browser, content scoped to your people.

track.note: Repo, test corpus, spec system, container readers, storage core, archive layer, the CLI.
Hex-level detective work on real game files. Code only ever gets written from these.
One per format — read a chunk into clean objects, write it back byte-identical.
Decoded chunks become things a person recognises: objects, sims, lots, families.
The platform's face, backed by the real store — browse, cards, thumbnails, the viewer.
Money, names, bios, skills and personality — all editable, all reversible.
Scan what you point it at, triage conflicts, enable and disable safely.
A WebGPU renderer — lots, walls, objects, animated Sims, in the browser.
The top of the pyramid. Groundwork committed; parked until the rest matures.

recent: The save editor writes: money, names, bios, object identity, skills and personality — one mutation flow, every commit byte-verified against a kept snapshot.
Cooking 0 → 300 → 0 on a real save reproduced the byte-exact original hash. Provably reversible.
Every one of the 248 lots now shows the house picture the game itself last drew.
A house join that took 15.2 seconds now takes 157 milliseconds.
